analysis.one_liner: Bars health insurers from denying coverage or setting premiums based on a person's health history.
analysis.headline: Introduced with no cosponsors in the final weeks of the session, the bill never received a hearing or vote and died in committee when Congress adjourned.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written national standards into the Social Security Act barring health insurers and employer plans from denying, limiting, or pricing coverage based on a person's health status, claims history, or medical history. It would have capped preexisting-condition exclusions at six months, credited prior coverage toward that waiting period, and generally required insurers to renew coverage for individuals and small employers. Enforcement would have run through state insurance commissioners, with federal fines as a backstop and grants to states to run enforcement programs.
analysis.who_benefits: People with medical histories — the ones insurers could refuse, price out, or drop — plus small employers and self-employed individuals who face the same underwriting. Anyone buying individual coverage or working for a small firm gains protection from being charged more or shut out because of past illness.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with health problems and small employers

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits insurers and group health plans from denying, limiting, or conditioning coverage and benefits, or varying premiums, based on health status, claims experience, medical history, or receipt of health care [S2] [S3].
Caps preexisting-condition exclusions at six months, reduces the exclusion month-for-month for people who had continuous prior coverage, and exempts newborns and pregnancy-related care entirely [S3].

Bars insurers from refusing to renew coverage for individuals or small employers except for narrow reasons such as nonpayment, fraud, or misrepresentation; an insurer that exits a market must give 180 days' notice and stay out of that market for five years [S3].

Requires each state's insurance commissioner to run an enforcement program, authorizes federal grants for state enforcement, and imposes federal civil money penalties of $150 per person per day when a state program falls short [S2] [S3].
Extends the same standards to employer group health plans through Department of Labor enforcement under ERISA [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and HMOs would lose the ability to screen applicants by health status and to drop or refuse renewal of costly policyholders, and would face federal fines for violations. Some of that cost would likely show up in higher premiums for healthy enrollees, the trade-off of spreading risk across everyone.

drawbacks.text: The bill still permits preexisting-condition exclusions of up to six months, and someone with a gap in coverage of more than three months loses credit for prior coverage — so people who were already uninsured could still wait months before their condition is covered [S3].
It allows premiums to vary by age, sex, and geographic area, so older people and women could still be charged substantially more [S3].

Insurers could stop enrolling anyone new in an area if they show capacity limits, and could exit a market outright with 180 days' notice, which in areas with few insurers could leave people without options [S3].

Enforcement depends first on state insurance commissioners, with federal penalties capped and waivable where a failure was due to reasonable cause — a structure critics of state-based enforcement say invites uneven protection [S3].

The definition of small employer covers firms with more than one but fewer than 50 employees, leaving purely solo self-employed workers outside the guaranteed-renewal and small-group protections [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection — barring insurers from denying or pricing coverage based on health history and requiring renewal — addresses one of the most damaging practices in the individual and small-group insurance market, and similar ideas later drew broad support. The bill is a modest version, though: it keeps preexisting-condition exclusions, allows rating by age and sex, and relies heavily on state enforcement. The main cost falls on insurers, with some of it likely passed into premiums for healthy customers; the main risk for patients is that in thin markets, insurers could exit rather than comply.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late November 1994, referred to two committees and then to subcommittees, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. James A. Hayes introduced the bill on November 29, 1994, in the final weeks of the 103rd Congress [S1] [S5].
It was referred jointly to the Energy and Commerce and Education and Labor committees on the day of introduction [S5].

On December 14, 1994, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment and the Subcommittee on Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness; no committee or subcommittee acted on it further [S5].
The 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, and the bill expired without any vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and HMOs came out ahead: they kept the ability to screen applicants by health status, price by medical history, and refuse or drop coverage for individuals and small employers, at least until comparable rules reached the statute book by other means.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers kept their underwriting freedom

for.name: Rep. James A. Hayes
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it; had no cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or reported the bill; referred it to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment, where it sat.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or reported the bill after receiving the referral.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, and never reached a vote, so no partisan split is visible in the record [S4].

industries.note: The bill would strip insurers of their ability to reject applicants, vary premiums, or refuse renewal based on health status and claims history, and expose them to federal fines — practices whose profits came at the expense of people with medical histories. Individuals and small employers would gain the protection insurers would lose.
